items.stem: Why did Europeans flee to America in 19th century? Identify the correct reason from the following options:

options.label: C
options.text: To escape from the French Revolution

options.label: D
options.text: As an aftermath of the Vietnam War

items.answer: Until the nineteenth century poverty and hunger were common in Europe, cities were crowded and deadly diseases such as smallpox and plague were widespread. Thousands therefore fled Europe for America, where an escape from want and disease seemed possible. So the reason is poverty and diseases.

items.stem: How much span of time can be referred for globalisation?
items.answer: Globalisation as an economic system is usually dated to the period beginning about half a century ago, even though trade and cultural exchange are far older. The span commonly referred to is the last 50 years.

items.stem: When was the active coastal trade linked the Indus Valley Civilisations with present day West Asia?
items.answer: An active coastal trade tied the Indus valley civilisations to present day West Asia from very early times. The textbook dates this link to as early as 3000 BCE.

items.answer: The Bretton Woods system rested on fixed exchange rates anchored to a dollar convertible into gold. From the 1960s the cost of America's overseas involvements drained its finances and eroded its competitive strength, so the dollar could no longer hold confidence as the world's principal currency. That weakness is exactly what broke the fixed rate system and brought in floating rates, so both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion.

items.stem: What 'technology' helped in transporting perishable goods?

items.stem: Economists identify three types of movement of flows within international economic exchanges which one type does not exist among them?

(1) Spices from India and Southeast Asia were traded to Europe, and in return precious metals such as gold and silver flowed from Europe to Asia. (2) Along the same routes Christian missionaries travelled to Asia, carrying beliefs and ideas with them. Trade and cultural exchange therefore moved together along the Silk route.

items.stem: Why can the First World War be termed as first modern industrial war ? Give three reason.
items.answer: The First World War is called the first modern industrial war for these reasons: (a) it saw the use of machine guns, tanks, aircraft and the like, all products of modern large scale industries; (b) the scale of total death and destruction was very large; and (c) carrying millions of soldiers needed large warships and railway trains, which could only be manufactured in large scale industries.

items.stem: Define liberalisation. Mention two components of liberalisation.
items.answer: Liberalisation is the relaxation of all the rules and regulations that earlier restricted the growth of the private sector. Its two components are: (i) allowing the private sector to run industrial activities that were earlier restricted to the public sector, and (ii) relaxing all rules and regulations that restrict the growth of the private sector.

items.stem: What do you mean by the term GPL ?
items.answer: GPL stands for Globalisation, Privatisation and Liberalisation. (i) Globalisation is the merger of the economies of individual countries into a global economy. (ii) Privatisation is the transfer of ownership, control and management of almost all erstwhile public sector undertakings to the private sector, done phase-wise. (iii) Liberalisation is the removal of trade barriers by relaxing trade laws, import rules and so on — for example the creation of SEZs, with labour laws made lenient, giving way to a contract or indentured labour system.

items.stem: What do you know about WTO ? Write about it in brief (short).
items.answer: WTO stands for the World Trade Organisation. It was set up in 1995 at Geneva, Switzerland. An international institution was already working as an organisation of the UN, called GATT — the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade — set up in 1947, two years after the birth of the UNO. The WTO replaced GATT in 1995 and since then has worked independently, though attached to the UN to some extent.

items.stem:
Write any three factors (values) which played a crucial role in the decline export of Indian textiles.
or
Which three factors are responsible for the declining Indian textile export ?
items.answer: The factors that played a crucial role in the decline of Indian textile exports were: (i) the Industrial Revolution in Europe, (ii) taxes imposed on Indian textile goods, and (iii) duty free British textile goods — sent to Indian markets without any levy — which were comparably cheaper than Indian cotton made goods.
items.ocr: The book prints the question with an alternate wording introduced by ‘or’; both wordings are kept in the stem.

items.stem: Why did Fixed Exchange Rate system collapse in 1960s ? Give three reasons.
items.answer: The fixed exchange rate system collapsed because: (1) from the 1960s the rising cost of its overseas involvements weakened the US’s finances and competitive strength; (2) the US dollar no longer commanded confidence as the world’s principal currency; and (3) it could not maintain its value in relation to gold, which led to the collapse of the fixed exchange rates.

items.stem: Examine different factors which led people to migrate to the continents of America and Australia in the nineteenth century.
items.answer: People migrated to America and Australia in the nineteenth century because: (i) acquiring agricultural land and getting better accommodation in these continents was a powerful attraction for the poor and backward people of poor countries; and (ii) better trade, commerce and industrial opportunities in America and Australia also inspired migrants from Asia, Africa and Latin America.
items.concept: Three flows of the world economy

items.stem: Write any three negative aspects of liberalisation and globalisation.
items.answer: Negative aspects of liberalisation and globalisation include: (i) the rate of unemployment increased beyond expectations; (ii) the growth rate declined to 4% per annum in 2002–03 from 8% in 1972–73; (iii) the laws failed to reduce the concentration of economic power in the private sector; and (iv) public sector enterprises ran into severe losses, to the tune of ₹ 203 crore, because of corruption, inefficiency and ineffective management.
items.ocr: The printed solution reads ‘unemployment increased below expectations’, which contradicts the sense of a negative aspect — read as ‘beyond expectations’. The rupee sign in ‘Z 203 crore’ is a font substitution for ₹. The book asks for three aspects but prints four.

items.stem: Describe the role of different religious groups in the development of anti-colonial feelings in Vietnam.
items.answer: Religion played an important part in building anti-colonial feeling in Vietnam. Vietnamese religious belief was a blend of Buddhism, Confucianism and local practices, so when the French introduced Christianity the Vietnamese reacted sharply and were angered by it. As a result an early anti-Christian movement, the Scholars' Revolt, broke out in 1868, led by officials of the Imperial Court who resented the spread of Christianity and of French power. The French suppressed the revolt, but the uprising inspired other patriots to rise against them; the Hoa Hao movement led by Huynh Phu So in the Mekong delta in 1939 was likewise significant in the growth of the anti-colonial movement.
items.ocr: The book prints this Vietnam question inside chapter 3 'Making of a Global World'; it belongs to the Vietnam/nationalism chapter and no concept in the chapter list matches it. Recorded as printed and mapped to the nearest concept, 'Decolonisation and development'.

items.stem: Describe the economic conditions of Britain after the 'First World War'.
items.answer: Britain, the leading economy of the pre-war world, went through a prolonged crisis after the First World War. To pay for war expenditure it had borrowed heavily from the United States, so the war ended with Britain carrying huge external debts. The war had also loosened its hold on the Indian market, where the nationalist movement had grown and anti-British feeling had spread among ordinary people, and where promoting Indian industry had become a nationalist aim, which hurt British industry. At home unemployment rose sharply while agricultural and industrial production fell; cotton production collapsed and cotton exports dropped dramatically. Unable to modernise, Britain found it hard to compete internationally with the United States, Germany and Japan.
items.concept: Economic impact of the First World War

items.stem: Briefly discuss the merits of globalisation and write three steps which have been taken by government to promote it in India.
items.answer: Merits of globalisation: it allows goods and services to flow freely across the world because trade barriers are reduced; it allows technology and experience to move freely between countries; it allows capital to flow freely among nations; and to some extent it allows labour to move to different countries. Steps taken by the Government of India to promote globalisation: trade barriers have been lifted since 1991 under a free trade policy adopted under pressure from the Ministerial Conference of the World Trade Organisation, an agency of the United Nations; technology and experience are being exchanged with several countries; restrictions on imports and exports have been minimised and taxes on imported goods reduced; and both central and state governments encourage investors from abroad to invest in India.

items.stem: Explain the causes of the Great Depression.
items.answer: The main causes of the Great Depression were the following. First, agricultural over-production: as farm prices and farm incomes fell, farmers tried to make up the loss by producing still more, which pushed prices down further and left produce rotting in the market for want of buyers, deepening their hardship. Second, the financial dependence of many countries on the United States: many countries had taken loans from the US, which were easy to raise while conditions were good, but by 1929 US overseas lenders panicked at the first sign of trouble and stopped lending to European countries, halting production there. Third, financial collapse: banks failed, currencies such as the British pound-sterling collapsed, and agricultural and raw material prices slumped, while the US government doubled import duties to protect its own economy, which dealt world trade another severe blow.

items.stem: What was the contribution of Christopher Columbus?
items.answer: Christopher Columbus discovered the vast continent that later came to be known as the Americas. With that discovery began cultural exchange with the original inhabitants of the continent. Foods such as potatoes, maize, tomatoes, chillies and sweet potatoes, unknown to people of other continents, were carried out of the Americas and became part of everyday diets elsewhere. From the sixteenth century the vast lands, abundant crops and minerals of America began to transform trade and lives everywhere, and precious metals, particularly silver from mines in present-day Peru and Mexico, enhanced Europe's wealth and financed its trade with Asia.

items.stem:
How did Silk Routes link the world ? Explain with three suitable examples.
or
Describe any three features of Silk Routes.
items.answer: The Silk Routes linked the world in the following ways. First, they are a good example of vibrant pre-modern trade and of cultural links between distant parts of the world. Second, the name 'Silk Routes' itself points to the importance of west-bound Chinese silk cargoes carried along the route. Third, historians have identified several silk routes, over land and by sea, which knitted together vast regions of Asia and linked Asia with Europe and northern Africa; they existed from before the Christian Era and thrived almost till the fifteenth century. Chinese pottery travelled the same routes, as did textiles and spices from India and Southeast Asia, while in return precious metals, gold and silver, flowed from Europe to Asia.

items.stem: Describe three types of flows or movements identified by the economists. What were the effects of these flows ?
items.answer: Economists identify three types of flows within international economic exchanges: the flow of trade, which in the nineteenth century largely meant trade in goods; the flow of labour, that is the migration of people in search of employment; and the flow, or movement, of capital invested over short or long distances. The effects were far-reaching. All three flows were closely interwoven and affected people's lives more deeply than ever before. The interconnections could sometimes be broken, for example when restrictions were placed on the migration of labour while goods and capital moved more freely. Looking at the three flows together helps us understand the nineteenth-century world economy better.
items.concept: Three flows of the world economy

items.stem: Write a short note on Indian entrepreneurs settled abroad.
items.answer: Indian bankers and traders who settled abroad financed trade across the world. Bankers such as the Shikaripuri Shroffs and the Nattukottai Chettiars used their own funds or funds borrowed from bankers in European countries, and financed corporate offices and organisations in India as well as the export of agricultural produce from Central and Southeast Asia. Indian traders and moneylenders, such as the Hyderabadi traders, opened emporia and offices for bulk sale in almost every seaport of the colonies across Europe and Africa, where they sold local agricultural produce, handicrafts, curios and antiques.

items.stem: Enlist the reasons because of which need for new economic policy was felt in India. Also write its objectives.
items.answer: The reasons that prompted the need for a New Economic Policy were the increase in the fiscal deficit, the increase in the deficit on the balance of payments, the Gulf crisis, the fall in exchange reserves, the rise in prices, and the poor performance of public sector undertakings. Its main objectives were the liberalisation of the economy, dispensing with too many controls, the expansion of the private sector, the encouragement of private foreign investment, the modernisation of agriculture, and control of the fiscal deficit.

items.stem: What were the aspects of New Economic Policy adopted in India ?
items.answer: The New Economic Policy began a process of economic reform in July 1991, and its main thrust was the liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation of the economy. All industries except four were freed from licensing, the ceiling of ₹100 crore on maximum investment by a company was removed, and most restrictions on direct foreign investment were lifted. Limits on users of foreign exchange were liberalised, and as a step towards privatisation newer areas were opened to the private sector. Only five industries remained reserved for the public sector, and as a step towards globalisation domestic industry was exposed to competition from multinational companies, with imports of capital goods and technology allowed.
items.ocr: The printed text shows the currency symbol as 'Z 100 corers'; read as ₹100 crore, a font-substitution artefact in the book.

items.stem: What are the monetary reforms under the New Economic Policy ?
items.answer: Under the New Economic Policy several monetary steps were taken on the recommendations of the Narasimham Committee: the direct credit programme was abolished, interest rates were freely determined, the banking system was reconstituted, banks were given more freedom, the accounting system was improved, and the liquidity ratio was reduced.

items.stem: Discuss the positive aspects of globalisation and liberalisation.
items.answer: Globalisation and liberalisation brought several positive results. They helped bring about rapid economic development, creating a large industrial base and increasing industrial production. The proportion of people living below the poverty line was reduced, self-sufficiency in food was achieved, and savings were mobilised. Resources for development were generated, a large pool of scientists and technically skilled persons was formed, and export-oriented units were established.

items.stem: What were the main sources of attraction for Europeans to come to Africa in the late nineteenth century ? How did they exploit their resources ?
items.answer: Europeans were drawn to Africa in the late nineteenth century by its vast resources of land and minerals. They came hoping to establish plantations and mines that would produce crops and minerals for export to Europe. To get the labour these needed, inheritance laws were changed so that peasants were displaced from the land, only one member of a family being allowed to inherit it, with the result that the others were pushed into the labour market. The Europeans also divided the different regions of Africa among themselves.
items.concept: Rinderpest and colonial control in Africa

items.stem: Explain the role of technology in shaping the world economy of the 19th century.
items.answer: Technology shaped the nineteenth-century world economy in three main ways. First, through changes in transport and communication: railways, steam shipping and the telegraph were inventions without which the transformation of the nineteenth-century world cannot be imagined. Second, by linking the various markets of the world: new investment and improvement in transport, faster railways, lighter wagons and larger ships moved food more cheaply and quickly from distant farms to final markets. Third, through its impact on the meat trade: until the 1870s meat was shipped from America to Europe as live animals that were slaughtered on arrival, which took up much ship space, and many animals died in the voyage, fell ill, lost weight or became unfit to eat, so meat prices were high and beyond the reach of the European poor and demand and production stayed low; the invention of refrigerated ships made it possible to carry meat itself from one region to another.
items.concept: Three flows of the world economy

items.stem: Discuss the darker side of expanding international trade and globalisation in late 19th century.
items.answer: Trade flourished and markets expanded in the late nineteenth century, but this was not only a period of expanding trade and growing prosperity; it had a darker side. First, loss of freedom and livelihood: in many parts of the world the expansion of trade and the closer relationship with the world economy also meant the loss of people's freedoms and livelihoods. Second, the division of Africa among imperialist powers: in 1885 the big European powers met in Berlin to complete the carving up of Africa between them. Third, the rise of colonial powers at the cost of colonised peoples: Britain and France made vast additions to their overseas territories in the late nineteenth century, and Belgium, Germany and the United States also became colonial powers.
items.concept: Rinderpest and colonial control in Africa

items.stem: What is Group 77 ? Why did Group 77 countries demand a New International Economic Order? Explain.
items.answer: The Group of 77 is a group of 77 developing countries that organised themselves as a separate bloc in order to share in the benefits of the fast growth the western economies experienced in the twenty to twenty-five years after the Second World War. They demanded a New International Economic Order for these reasons: to gain real control over their own natural resources; to obtain more development assistance from the advanced western countries; to secure better and fairer prices for their raw materials; and to win better access for their manufactured goods in the markets of the developed countries.

items.stem: Explain the impact of the First World War on Britain.
items.answer: Post-war economic recovery proved difficult for Britain because the heavy expenditure on the First World War had weakened the British economy. While Britain was preoccupied with the war, industries developed in Japan and India, so Britain now had to face competition from these countries, especially from Japan. To finance war expenditure Britain had borrowed liberally from the United States, which meant that at the end of the war it was burdened with huge external debts. The war had also brought an economic boom, that is a large increase in demand, production, prices and employment; when the war boom ended production contracted and unemployment increased.
items.concept: Economic impact of the First World War

items.stem: Why was there a need for clearing lands in Britain during the 19th century ? Explain any three reasons.
items.answer: Land tracts were cleared in Britain for several reasons, of which three are important. First, the increasing demand for food-grains: Britain's population grew very fast in the late phase of the eighteenth century, so the demand for food-grains rose, and land was cleared to expand the area of farming and meet the need for eatables, food-grains, vegetables and fruit. Second, the introduction and expansion of the railways: it was not enough merely to clear land for agriculture, since railways were needed to link the agricultural regions to the ports, so land was cleared to lay new railway lines. Third, homes and settlements: people had to settle on the land in order to bring it under cultivation, and this meant building homes and settlements.
items.concept: Three flows of the world economy
items.ocr: The printed stem carries a stray opening quotation mark, 'during the 19th century ?'; transcribed without it.

items.stem:
Describe the effects of the Great Depression of 1929 on the United States of America.
or
'The US was severely affected by the Great Depression of 1929.' Justify the statement with examples.
items.answer: The United States was greatly affected by the Great Depression of 1929. With the fall in prices, US banks slashed domestic lending and called back loans. Many houses and businesses collapsed. Faced with falling incomes, many households could not repay their loans and had to give up their houses, cars and other consumer durables. Unemployment soared and people trudged long distances looking for work. Unable to recover their investments and loans or to repay depositors, thousands of banks went bankrupt and were forced to close: by 1933 over 4,000 banks had closed and 110,000 companies had collapsed.

items.stem: Describe the explosive conditions prevailed in Balkans after 1871 in Europe.
items.answer: After 1871 the Balkans became the most explosive region of Europe. The Balkans was a region of great geographical and ethnic variation, covering modern Romania, Bulgaria, Albania, Greece, Macedonia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Slovenia, Serbia and Montenegro, whose inhabitants were broadly known as the Slavs. Much of the area was under Ottoman rule, and through the nineteenth century the Ottoman Empire tried to strengthen itself by modernisation and internal reform but with very little success. One by one its European subject nationalities broke away from its control and declared themselves independent. These Balkan peoples based their claims to independence and political rights on nationality, using history to prove that they had once been independent and had later been subjugated by foreign powers. Each rebellious nationality therefore saw its struggle as an attempt to win back a long lost independence, and as the various Slavic groups fought one another over territory, and the big European powers backed rival claims in the race for trade, colonies and naval strength, the region was converted into a battleground.
items.concept: Economic impact of the First World War

items.stem: Illustrate with examples that food offers many opportunities of long-distance cultural exchange.
items.answer: Food shows very clearly how distant cultures have exchanged with one another. Traders and travellers introduced new crops to every land they reached, so that ready foodstuff in distant parts of the world often share a common origin. Many of our commonest foods — potatoes, maize, soya, groundnuts, tomatoes, chillies and sweet potatoes — came to Europe and Asia from the Americas, and were unknown to our ancestors until about five centuries ago. It is believed that noodles travelled west from China to become 'spaghetti', or perhaps Arab traders carried pasta to fifth century Sicily, an island in Italy. Indian 'rotis' have become 'tortillas' in Mexico, America and other western countries. Similar foods were also known in India and Japan, so the truth about their origin may never be settled, yet the very guesswork suggests how much long-distance cultural contact there was even in the pre-modern world. The consequences could be dramatic: with the introduction of the potato Europe's poor began to eat better and live longer, and the poor of Ireland became so dependent on it that when disease destroyed the potato crop in the 1840s a large number of people died of starvation. Food, therefore, is one of the clearest records of long-distance cultural exchange.

items.stem: “Even before factories began to dot the landscape in England and Europe, there was large-scale industrial production for an international market in the country side.” Elucidate.
items.answer: The seventeenth and eighteenth centuries were a time when open fields were disappearing and commons were being enclosed. Cottagers and poor peasants who had earlier depended on common land for survival — gathering firewood, berries, vegetables, hay and straw — now had to look for alternative sources of income. Many had only tiny plots of land that could not employ all the members of the household, so when merchants arrived and offered advances to produce goods for them, they happily agreed. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries merchants from the towns of Europe began moving to the countryside, supplying money to peasants and artisans and persuading them to produce for an international market. With the expansion of world trade and the acquisition of colonies in different parts of the world the demand for goods was growing, but merchants could not expand production within the towns because urban crafts and trade guilds were powerful there. The guilds were associations of producers that trained craftspeople, maintained control over production, regulated competition and prices and restricted the entry of new people into a trade, and rulers had granted different guilds the monopoly right to produce and trade in specific products, so it was very difficult for a new merchant to set up business in a town. This is why merchants turned to the countryside, where poor peasants and artisans who had lost their common lands began working for them. In this way large-scale industrial production for an international market was already being carried on in the villages, long before factories dotted the landscape.
items.ocr: Proto-industrialisation question printed in this chapter; nearest available concept used.

items.stem: “The function and the shape of the family were completely transformed by life in the industrial city.” Clarify the statement with regard to urbanization that happened in England in the 18th century.
items.answer: In the eighteenth century the family had been a unit of production and of consumption as well as of political decision-making, and life in the industrial city broke that older pattern completely. Ties between members of the household loosened, and among the working class the institution of marriage tended to break down. Women of the upper and middle classes in Britain, on the other hand, faced increasingly higher levels of isolation, although their lives were made easier by domestic maids who cooked, cleaned and cared for young children on low wages. Women who worked for wages did gain some control over their own lives, particularly among the lower social classes; but many social reformers felt that the family as an institution had broken down and needed to be saved or reconstructed by pushing these women back into their homes. The city also encouraged a new spirit of individualism among both men and women and a freedom from the collective values that had been a feature of the smaller rural communities. Men and women, however, did not have equal access to this new urban space: as women lost their industrial jobs and conservative people rallied against their presence in public places, women were forced to withdraw into their homes. Thus both the function and the shape of the family were transformed by the industrial city.
items.ocr: Urbanisation question printed in this chapter; no matching concept in the list, so the broadest available concept was used.

items.stem: Describe any five factors that led to the end of the Bretton Woods system and the beginning of globalisation.
items.answer: The Bretton Woods system came apart for several connected reasons. First, from the 1960s the rising costs of its overseas involvements weakened the finances and the competitive strength of the United States. Second, the US dollar no longer commanded confidence as the world's principal currency. Third, the dollar could not maintain its fixed value in relation to gold, which was the anchor of the whole arrangement. Fourth, this eventually led to the collapse of the system of fixed exchange rates and to the introduction of a system of floating exchange rates. Fifth, the international financial system itself changed in important ways: developing countries were now forced to borrow from western commercial banks and private lending institutions instead of from the Bretton Woods institutions, which brought periodic debt crises and lower incomes. Finally, the industrial world was hit by unemployment, and multinational companies began shifting production to low-wage countries, above all to China, whose cheap labour made it a favoured destination. Together these developments ended the Bretton Woods order and opened the era of globalisation.
items.ocr: Question asks for five factors; the printed answer lists six.

items.stem: Explain the statement ‘the food travels throughout the world’ with examples.
items.answer: That food travels throughout the world is a historical fact. Trade in goods, including foodgrains, always carried long-distance cultural exchange with it: traders and travellers introduced new crops to the lands they visited, so that even rare foodstuffs in far apart parts of the world may share a common origin. Spaghetti and noodles are the standard example — it is believed that noodles travelled west from China to become spaghetti, or perhaps Arab traders took pasta to fifth century Sicily, an island now in Italy. Similar foods were also known in India and Japan, and are so ancient there that their origins may never be established; such guesswork itself suggests the possibilities of long-distance cultural contact even in the pre-modern world. Many of our common foods — potatoes, soya, groundnuts, maize, tomatoes, chillies and sweet potatoes — were not known to our ancestors until about five centuries ago. They were introduced into Europe and Asia only after Christopher Columbus incidentally discovered the vast continent later known as the Americas, including North America, South America and the Caribbean. Food therefore travels with people, and the world's kitchens are a record of that travel.

items.stem:
Why has the indentured labour system in 19th century been described as a new system of slavery ?
or
Nineteenth century indenture has been described on a new system of slavery. Explain three reasons.
items.answer: Nineteenth century indenture is called a new system of slavery because, although the labourer signed a contract, in practice he was bound and exploited much as a slave was. It was a world of faster economic growth but also of greater misery — higher incomes for some and poverty for others, technological advance in some areas and new forms of exploitation in others. Most indentured workers migrated in the hope of a bright future, but they were exploited both by the recruiting agent and by the employer. They had to pay a commission to the recruiting agent out of their meagre earnings. The agents routinely gave false information about the final destination, the modes of travel, the nature of the work and the living and working conditions, so that the worker agreed to terms he did not understand. Sometimes agents even forcibly abducted less willing migrants. Once on the plantation the worker's legal rights were minimal and he could not leave before the contract ended. For all these reasons the system, though formally contractual, amounted to a new form of slavery.

items.stem: Write any three factors responsible for indentured labour migration from India.
items.answer: Indentured labour was bonded labour working under contract for an employer for a specified period, and several factors pushed such migration out of India. First, the world order of the time was one of domination and slavery: Europeans grew steadily wealthier while the people of Asian and African countries suffered misery, exploitation and poverty at the same time. Second, the colonial economy at home was collapsing — cottage industries in India declined, rates of land revenue rose, and peasants were displaced by Europeans setting up large-scale industries; these pressures forced Indian peasants to migrate to other countries as indentured labourers. Third, there was a strong pull from abroad, because the demand for labour was high in Trinidad, Guyana and Surinam in the Caribbean and in Mauritius and Fiji, where plantations needed cheap workers. This produced a large-scale flow of labour from the East to the West, and a contract labour system emerged in which middlemen, of the kind already seen in the slave trade, recruited and controlled the workers, as was plain from the behaviour of British plantation owners and miners towards indentured labourers during the contract period.

items.stem: How was the food problem solved in Britain after the scrapping of the ‘Corn Laws’ ? Explain.
items.answer: After the Corn Laws were scrapped, Britain solved its food problem in three ways. First, foodgrains and other eatables were imported. Once the restriction was gone, foodgrains and all kinds of food items were brought in from abroad, and they were cheaper than anything that could be produced within Britain; British traders and merchants began importing cheap food from Australia, the USA, Russia and some eastern European countries. Second, a new shape was given to the agricultural economy. A global agricultural economy took hold, for the large-scale import of foodgrains made food a world commodity: food no longer came from a nearby town or village but from thousands of miles away. In the exporting regions large farms were created and cultivated with new agricultural machines and tools, and these farms were linked to the ports by railways, roads and waterways. Third, networks of irrigation were built in Britain's colonies: the British colonial government in India and elsewhere constructed networks of irrigation canals that transformed semi-desert wastes into fertile agricultural land capable of growing wheat and cotton for export to Britain. In this way cheap food from a world-wide supply area replaced the protected home supply.
items.concept: Three flows of the world economy

items.stem: Discuss the main characteristics related with First World Wartime transformation.
items.answer: The First World War transformed the world in several basic ways. It was the first modern industrial war, born of the industrial interests of the big powers, and it saw machine guns, tanks, aircraft and chemical weapons used on a massive scale. It caused a great shortage of men of working age, because most of those killed and injured were men of working age, and these deaths and injuries reduced the able-bodied workforce of Europe. It brought women workers into the service and industrial sectors: industries were restructured to produce war-related goods, entire societies were reorganised for war, and as men went to battle women stepped into jobs in factories, offices, schools and hospitals. Finally, it reversed the financial standing of the great powers — Britain became a debtor and the United States became an international creditor. The war shattered markets, the agricultural production Europeans had earlier maintained slumped, and money had to be borrowed from American banks and the American public. These are the main characteristics of the wartime transformation.
items.concept: Economic impact of the First World War
items.ocr: Question stem printed at the foot of page 19; the answer runs on page 20.

items.stem: How did the First World War change the economic life of the people in Britain ? Explain.
items.answer: The First World War had a great impact on the economic life of Britain. First, there was heavy expenditure: Britain had to fight on several fronts and bore very heavy costs during the war years, so post-war economic recovery proved very difficult and the war weakened the British economy. Second, Britain faced new industrial competition. While she was preoccupied with the war, industries had developed in Japan and India, and Britain now had to face competition from these countries, especially from Japan. Third, there was a heavy loan burden owed to the USA: to finance war expenditure Britain had borrowed liberally from the United States, so that at the end of the war she was burdened with huge external debts. Fourth, economic depression followed. Prices of most commodities had risen during the war; afterwards several industrial units closed down, unemployment increased and exports of many items fell. Some banks, insurance companies and financial institutions were forced to declare themselves bankrupt under the adverse impact of the Economic Depression that came out of the USA between 1929 and 1933. Together these changes left the British people poorer, more indebted and more exposed to unemployment than before the war.
items.concept: Economic impact of the First World War

items.stem: What do you know about World Trade Organisation? Explain.
items.answer: The World Trade Organisation (WTO) was set up under the United Nations to promote international trade among countries, and its headquarters is at Geneva. It was established on 1 January 1995 and by January 2002 had 144 member countries; India became a member on 1 January 1995. The WTO replaced the General Agreement on Trade and Tariffs (GATT), which had been established in 1948. It has significantly influenced the process of liberalisation in the world. The organisation is based on the principle of discrimination-free trade and the promotion of fair competition among member nations. Most of its rules are framed on the basis of persuasion and its decisions are taken by consensus; the Ministerial Conference is its law-making body, though the USA has considerable hegemony there. The WTO wants both import and export quotas to be abolished and wants countries to follow multinational agreements, and all its members have adopted laws and policies in order to comply with WTO rules.

items.stem: Why liberalisation has been adopted in India ? Mention freedoms given to private sector under it. Also enlist main measures undertaken for liberalisation of economy in our country since 1991.
items.answer: India adopted liberalisation to achieve three objectives: to free Indian industry from needless and irksome controls, to upgrade technology, and to develop international competitiveness. The freedoms given to the private sector under liberalisation were these: industrial licensing was abolished except for five priority industries; the number of public sector industries was reduced from 17 to 3; and industry was freed from regulations such as the need for permission to import raw materials. The main measures undertaken for the liberalisation of the Indian economy since 1991 were the abolition of industrial licensing and registration, concessions from the Monopolies Act, freedom for industries to expand and to raise production, an increase in the investment limit of small industries, freedom to import capital goods, freedom to import technology, and free determination of interest rates. Taken together these steps replaced a permit-based economy with one in which the private sector chose its own scale, technology and markets.

items.stem: Describe the main changes that took place due to Liberalisation and Globalisation.
items.answer: The changes brought by liberalisation and globalisation can be classified into visible changes and invisible changes. The visible changes were felt directly by consumers: far better services in the telecommunication sector, and colour television sets and other electronic goods available at low prices; and the market for cold drinks and food products being taken over by companies such as Pepsi and Coca-Cola. The invisible changes were structural. India's share in the world trade of goods and services increased. Investment from foreign countries rose sharply, from ₹174 crores in 1991 to ₹9,338 crores in 2000, and foreign exchange needed to pay for imports grew from ₹4,822 crores in 1991 to ₹1,59,924 crores in 2000. New jobs were created, but not in sufficient numbers to meet all the needs, especially in the rural sector, and the growth of industry did not reach the level that had been expected. Thus liberalisation and globalisation brought visible consumer gains along with mixed results for employment and industrial growth.
items.ocr: The printed rupee figures use a mis-set glyph 'Z' for ₹; transcribed as ₹.

items.stem: Describe any five measures of liberalisation taken by the Government of India.
items.answer: The Government of India took the following measures of liberalisation. First, industries were exempted from licensing: the private sector has been freed to set up all industries except a few, without any kind of industrial licence. Second, permission was given to import raw material from abroad — under the new economic policy companies can import raw materials and government permission is no longer required. Third, the investment limit of small industries was extended, the restriction on investment by large business having been lifted. Fourth, the concept of MRTP was done away with, so that there are now no MRTP companies and firms can take their own investment decisions and expansion plans. Fifth, industries were allowed to expand freely according to the needs of the market, the ceiling on capital having been abolished. Sixth, the number of industries reserved for the public sector was reduced from 7 to 3, so that the private sector can now enter core industries such as iron and steel, electricity, air transport, shipbuilding, heavy machinery and some defence goods.
items.ocr: Question asks for five measures; the printed answer lists six.

items.stem: What was the main aim of the post-war international economic system? Mention the two Bretton Woods Institutions established in 1944 with their main objectives.
items.answer: The main aim of the post-war international economic system was to preserve economic stability and full employment in the industrial world. Economists and politicians had drawn two key lessons from inter-war economic experience. First, an industrial society is based on mass consumption. Second, to ensure mass consumption there had to be high and stable incomes, and incomes could not be stable unless employment was stable; thus stable incomes also require steady, full employment. Since markets alone could not guarantee full employment, governments would have to step in to minimise fluctuations of price, output and employment, so that economic stability could be ensured only through the intervention of the government. The framework of this programme was agreed upon at the United Nations Monetary and Financial Conference held in July 1944 at Bretton Woods in New Hampshire, USA. Two institutions were established there: the International Monetary Fund, whose objective was to deal with the external surpluses and deficits of its member nations, and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, the World Bank, set up to finance post-war reconstruction. The Bretton Woods system inaugurated an era of unprecedented growth of trade and income for the western industrial nations and Japan.

items.stem:
‘G-77 can be seen as a reaction to the activities of Bretton Woods Twins’. Explain the statement with three arguments.
or
Describe the circumstances responsible for the formation of G-77.
items.answer: It is rightly said that the G-77 can be seen as a reaction to the activities of the Bretton Woods twins. The Bretton Woods twins, the IMF and the World Bank, were dominated by the former colonial powers, so most developing countries did not benefit from the fast growth that the western economies experienced in the 1950s and 1960s; they therefore organised themselves as a group, the Group of 77 or G-77, to demand a New International Economic Order. The former colonial powers continued to exploit the natural resources of developing nations through the IMF and the World Bank, and the developing nations organised themselves into the G-77 so as to gain real control over their own natural resources. They also wanted more developmental assistance and fairer prices for the raw materials they sold, and a better opportunity for their manufactured goods in the markets of the developed nations. The G-77 was thus the collective answer of the newly independent countries to an international economic order that had been built without them.

items.stem: ‘The impact of Great Depression of 1929 was different on the Indian rural and industrial society.’ Justify the statement.
items.answer: The Great Depression of 1929 struck India, then under British rule, severely, but it fell very unevenly on the countryside and on the towns. The Government of British India adopted a protective trade policy which, though beneficial for the United Kingdom, caused great damage to the Indian economy. During 1929-1937 exports and imports fell drastically, crippling seaborne international trade, and the railways and the agricultural sector were the worst affected. Peasants and farmers suffered far more than urban dwellers: although agricultural prices fell sharply, the colonial government refused to reduce its revenue demands, and peasants producing for the world market were hit hardest of all. Across India peasants' indebtedness increased; they used up their savings, mortgaged their lands and sold jewellery and precious metals to meet daily expenses. For urban India, on the other hand, the depression was far less grim precisely because prices were falling. Those with fixed incomes — town-dwelling landowners who received rents and middle class salaried employees — found themselves better off, since everything cost less, and they also benefited from industrial investment, which grew because the government had extended tariff protection to industries. Thus the same depression ruined the rural producer while leaving urban India comparatively better placed.

The exchange of goods among people, states and countries is referred to as trade. The market is the place where such exchanges take place. Trade between two countries is called international trade. It may take place through sea, air or land routes. While local trade is carried in cities, towns and villages, state level trade is carried between two or more states. Advancement of international trade of a country is an index to its economic prosperity. It is, therefore, considered the economic barometer for a country.

As the resources are space bound, no country can survive without international trade. Export and import are the components of trade. The balance of trade of a country is the difference between its export and import. When the value of export exceeds the value of imports, it is called a favourable balance of trade. On the contrary, if the value of imports exceeds the value of exports, it is termed as unfavourable balance of trade.

India has trade relations with all the major trading blocks and all geographical regions of the world. The commodities exported from India to other countries include gems and jewellery, chemicals and related products, agriculture and allied products, etc.

The commodities imported to India include petroleum crude and products, gems and jewellery, chemicals and related products, base metals, electronic items, machinery, agriculture and allied products. India has emerged as a software giant at the international level and it is earning large foreign exchange through the export of information technology.

Questions :
1. What do you mean by international trade?
2. What is meant by favourable and unfavourable balance of trade?
3. What are the commodities export and imported by India in international trade?
items.answer:
1. The exchange of goods among people, states and countries is referred to as trade. Trade carried on between two countries is called international trade.
2. The balance of trade of a country is the difference between its exports and its imports. When the value of exports exceeds the value of imports it is a favourable balance of trade; when the value of imports exceeds the value of exports it is an unfavourable balance of trade.
3. Among India's exports in 2016-17 the share of agriculture and allied products was 8.64 per cent, base metals 6.91 per cent, gems and jewellery 17.02 per cent and chemicals and related products 12.06 per cent. The commodities imported into India in 2016-17 were petroleum crude and products 22.4 per cent, gems and jewellery 12.8 per cent, chemicals and related products 9.76 per cent, base metals 5.95 per cent, electronic items 10.94 per cent, machinery 8.9 per cent and agriculture and allied products 5.84 per cent.

items.stem:
Read the source given below and answer the questions that follows:

In Africa, in the 1890s, a fast-spreading disease of cattle plague or rinderpest had a terrifying impact on people's livelihoods and the local economy. This is a good example of the widespread European imperial impact on colonised societies. It shows how in this era of conquest even a disease affecting cattle, reshaped the lives and fortunes of thousands of people and their relations with the rest of the world. Historically, Africa had abundant land and a relatively small population. For centuries, land and livestock sustained African livelihoods and people rarely worked for a wage. In late nineteenth-century Africa, there were few consumer goods that wages could buy. If you had been an African possessing land and livestock - and there was plenty of both - you too would have seen little reason to work for a wage.

Questions :
1. What was Rinderpest?
2. What were the two main sources of African economy for past centuries?
3. How cattle plague affected the situation of people in Africa?
items.answer:
1. Rinderpest was a fast-spreading cattle plague that struck Africa in the 1890s and killed millions of cattle across the continent.
2. For several centuries the African economy rested mainly on land and livestock; Africans rarely worked for a wage.
3. The cattle plague was disastrous for Africans because the millions of livestock it killed were their source of livelihood. Stripped of their cattle, the people were turned into labourers by the colonisers, who paid them meagre wages for large amounts of manual work.
items.concept: Rinderpest and colonial control in Africa

items.stem:
Read the source given below and answer the questions that follows:

The Portuguese and Spanish conquest and colonisation of America was decisively under way by the mid-sixteenth century. European conquest was not just a result of superior firepower. In fact, the most powerful weapon of the Spanish conquerors was not a conventional military weapon at all. It was the germs such as those of smallpox that they carried on their person. Because of their long isolation, America's original inhabitants had no immunity against these diseases that came from Europe. Smallpox in particular proved a deadly killer. Once introduced, it spread deep into the continent, ahead even of any Europeans reaching there. It killed and decimated whole communities, paving the way for conquest.

Questions :
1. Which two nations were the earliest colonisers in America?
2. What were some of the reasons due to which the colonisers easily established their control over several parts of America?
3. How smallpox turned into death of native people of America?
items.answer:
1. Portugal and Spain were the earliest nations to colonise America, around the mid-sixteenth century.
2. The colonisers had superior firepower, military weapons and many advanced materials, but their most important weapon proved to be smallpox.
3. The Spanish conquerors carried smallpox and transmitted it to large numbers of native Americans, among whom it spread rapidly. Having lived in long isolation, the natives had no immunity to the disease, so thousands died; it wiped out whole communities and made colonisation easier.
items.concept: Disease as a weapon of conquest

items.stem:
Read the given extract and answer the following questions.

The Bretton Woods conference established the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to deal with external surpluses and deficits of its member nations. The International Bank for reconstruction and development (popularly known as the World Bank) was set up to finance post-war reconstruction: The IMF and the World Bank are referred to as the Bretton Woods institutions or sometimes the Bretton Woods twins. The post-war international economic system is also often described as the Bretton Woods system. The IMF and the World Bank commenced financial operations in 1947. Decision-making in these institutions is controlled by the Western industrial powers. The US has an effective right of vote over key IMF and World Bank decisions.

The International Monetary System is the system linking national currencies and monetary system. The Bretton Woods system was based on fixed exchange rates. In this system, national currencies, for example, the Indian rupees were pegged to the dollar at a fixed exchange rate. The dollar itself was anchored to gold at a fixed price of $35 per ounce of gold.

Questions :
1. What was the reason behind setting up of International Monetary Fund?
2. Describe the Bretton Woods System.
3. A significant decision was taken at Bretton Woods in New Hampshire. Explain.
items.answer:
1. The IMF was set up to promote international monetary cooperation and to deal with the external surpluses and deficits of its member nations.
2. The Bretton Woods System was based on fixed exchange rates. National currencies such as the Indian rupee were pegged to the dollar at a fixed exchange rate, and the dollar itself was anchored to gold at a fixed price of $35 per ounce of gold.
3. At the Bretton Woods Conference in New Hampshire, USA, it was decided to establish the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund to preserve global economic stability and full employment in the industrial world. These institutions would also deal with the surpluses and deficits of member nations and finance post-war reconstruction.

The example of indentured labour migration from India also illustrates the two-sided nature of the nineteenth-century world. It was a world of faster economic growth as well as great misery, higher incomes for some and poverty for others, technological advances in some areas and new forms of coercion in others.

Indian traders and moneylenders also followed European colonisers into Africa. Hyderabadi Sindhi traders, however, ventured beyond European colonies. From the 1860s they established flourishing emporia at busy ports worldwide, selling local and imported curios to tourists whose numbers were beginning to swell, thanks to the development of safe and comfortable passenger vessels.

Historically, fine cottons produced in India were exported to Europe. With industrialisation, British cotton manufacture began to expand and industrialists pressurised the government to restrict cotton imports and protect local industries. Tariffs were imposed on cloth imports into Britain. Consequently, the inflow of fine Indian cotton began to decline.

Questions :
1. What do you mean by indentured labour?
2. How did Indian traders flourished?
3. Why did Indian cotton begin to decline?
items.answer:
1. An indentured labourer is a bonded labourer under contract to work for an employer for a specific amount of time, in order to pay off his passage to a new country or home.
2. Indian traders established flourishing emporia at busy ports worldwide, selling local and imported curios to tourists whose numbers were beginning to swell.
3. With industrialisation British cotton manufacture expanded, and the industrialists pressurised the government to restrict cotton imports and protect local industries. Tariffs were imposed on cloth imports into Britain, and consequently the inflow of fine Indian cotton began to decline.

items.stem:
Read the extract and answer the questions that follows:

The Second World War broke out a mere two decades after the end of the First World War. It was fought between the Axis Powers (mainly Nazi Germany, Japan and Italy) and the Allies (Britain, France, the Soviet Union and the US). It was a war waged for six years on many fronts, in many places, over land, on sea, in the air. Once again death and destruction was enormous. At least 60 million people, or about 3 per cent of the world's 1939 population, is believed to have been killed, directly or indirectly, as a result of the war. Millions more were injured. Unlike in earlier wars, most of these deaths took place outside the battlefields. Many more civilians than soldiers died from war-related causes. Vast parts of Europe and Asia were devastated, and several cities were destroyed by aerial bombardment or relentless artillery attacks. The war caused an immense amount of economic devastation and social disruption. Reconstruction promised to be long and difficult. Two crucial influences shaped post-war reconstruction. The first was the US's emergence as the dominant economic, political and military power in the Western world. The second was the dominance of the Soviet Union. It had made huge sacrifices to defeat Nazi Germany, and transformed itself from a backward agricultural country into a world power during the very years when the capitalist world was trapped in the Great Depression.

Questions
1. Who were the countries directly involved in the Second World War?
2. Who trapped the world in the Great Depression?
3. What was the duration of the Second World War?
items.answer:
1. The Second World War was fought between the Axis Powers (mainly Nazi Germany, Japan and Italy) and the Allies (Britain, France, the Soviet Union and the US).
2. The capitalist world trapped the world in the Great Depression.
3. The war lasted six years, waged on many fronts and in many places, over land, on sea and in the air.
